land.text: Taebong's whole realm, taken over in the 918 coup that put Wang Kon on the throne

predecessors.note: Same state, new ruler and old name: 'Wang Kŏn was raised to the throne after Kung Ye was deposed' and restored the name Goryeo (Goryeo and Taebong pages). Cliopatria starts Goryeo in 922 with Taebong's outline.

land.text: Silla's remaining Gyeongsang region round Gyeongju, which Gyeongsun handed over in 935

predecessors.note: Not the same state: 'Gyeongsun submitted to Wang Geon of the emerging Goryeo in 935' (Unified Silla page); the Goryeo page has 'the peaceful annexation of Later Silla in 935'. The land is the 935 gain in the ledger.

land.text: Later Baekje: Jeolla and the south-west, conquered in 936

predecessors.note: Not the same state: 'Later Paekche thus finally fell in 936' (Later Baekje page); the Goryeo page has the 'Conquest of Later Baekje, 936'. The land is the 936 gain in the ledger.

land.text: all of Goryeo: Yi Sŏnggye 'put to death the last three Goryeo kings' and established Joseon in 1392

successors.note: Abdication of Gongyang 12 July 1392 (infobox). Cliopatria ends Goryeo in 1394 and starts Joseon in 1395.

capitals.name: Cheorwon
capitals.note: Infobox 'Cheorwon (918-919)', temporary. The text says Wang Kon 'moved the capital back to Kaesong'; the infobox year 919 is used for the move. Coordinates are the county seat of Cheorwon (the gazetteer has no entry).

capitals.name: Ganghwa
capitals.note: Infobox 'Ganghwa (1232-1270)': the court fled the Mongols; the return to the mainland was agreed in 1259 but 'would not happen until many years later' (Mongol invasions page).

correction.text: Taebong's outline from the coup of 918 plus Naju: Hwanghae, Gyeonggi, Gangwon, the Pyongyang region, the north of Chungcheong and the south-western city Wang Kon took in 910

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: Cliopatria's Goryeo starts in 922 but the page dates the founding to 918 ('Coronation of Taejo: 25 July 918'). The land is Taebong's, which Cliopatria draws in the Taebong row to 921 (identical 81,790 km2 outline). The Goryeo infobox gives no area. Fix round: Naju is added. 'Then in 910, when Wang Kŏn, the general of the rival kingdom of Majin, attacked and captured the city of Naju' and Kyŏn Hwŏn then 'made an attempt to retake the city from Wang by laying siege to it for ten days' (Gyeon Hwon page); Wang Kon is Taebong's general and then Goryeo's king, and hubaekje drops Naju from 910, so the city is Taebong's 911-917 (taebong_911) and Goryeo's from 918. Cliopatria's Taebong and Goryeo shapes stop north of it (southern limit 36.0 N).

81,790 km2, Taebong's outline, for 922-934. The page gives no area or boundary; it dates Later Baekje's attack on Gyeongju (927), the defeat near Daegu (927) and victories over Later Baekje in 930 and 934. Borders with Later Baekje and Silla are soft. Fix round: verdict ok became adjust: the outline is Taebong's and omits Naju, which Wang Kon captured in 910 ('attacked and captured the city of Naju', Gyeon Hwon page) and Later Baekje never retook, so Naju is Goryeo's from 918 (and nobody's 918-935 if the shape is left as drawn). Cliopatria's 936 shape holds it again.

correction.text: the Cliopatria 922 shape plus Naju; valid 922-934
unchanged Cliopatria 936 shape; valid 935-992 only (Silla annexed 935, Later Baekje conquered 936); from 993 use goryeo_993

keyframe_review.note: Cliopatria's 142,875 km2 whole-peninsula shape is right for 935-992 but starts a year late: the page has 'the peaceful annexation of Later Silla in 935' and the conquest of Later Baekje in 936. It stops at 39.45 N, which is too small for the later north (see goryeo_993). Years change only. [orchestrator 2 Nov 2026: from/to set to 935..992 from this entry's own 'valid 935-992 only'; without them the compiler drew the shape for all its Cliopatria years, overlapping the next keyframe (window p1100-p1199 report)]

correction.text: the 936 Cliopatria shape plus North Pyongan up to the Yalu

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe. 'Goryeo formally incorporated the land between the border of Liao and Goryeo up to the Yalu River' in 993, land the Jurchen tribes had occupied; the Goryeo page has Sŏ Hŭi building forts east of the Yalu in 994-996 and Cheolli Jangseong built 1033-1044 'from the mouth of the Yalu River to the east coast'. Cliopatria's shape never reaches the Yalu (North Pyongan is outside it). The 1014-1031 loss of the Poju (Uiju) region is a ledger event, not a keyframe.

correction.text: the Cliopatria 1139 shape plus North Pyongan up to the Yalu

keyframe_review.note: Cliopatria's shape (142,632 km2, 243 km2 smaller than 936) leaves out the Yalu frontier that the page dates to 993 and the Cheolli Jangseong wall of 1033-1044. The Jurchen swing of 1104-1108 is a ledger event. In 1126 the king 'declared himself a Jin vassal' (Goryeo page), a suzerain event for the Jin dossier.

correction.text: the Cliopatria 1216 shape plus North Pyongan up to the Yalu

keyframe_review.note: Same correction as goryeo_1139 (142,904 km2). 1216-1219: Khitans invaded Goryeo and allied Mongol-Goryeo forces finished them off in 1219; no land changed hands.

correction.text: the Cliopatria 1227 shape plus North Pyongan; the Mongol contest zone of 1231-1259 lies in the added part

keyframe_review.note: 142,632 km2 for 1227-1259. From 1231 the Mongols hold North Pyongan in part ('Mongol darughachis controlled almost all of modern North Pyongan Province' by 1232), so the added North Pyongan is the contest zone of the ledger from 1231 to 1259. Ssangseong (1258) is outside this shape. The court sat at Ganghwa from 1232.

correction.text: the Cliopatria 1227 shape plus North Pyongan

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: Cliopatria has no Goryeo shape for 1260-1362, though the state went on (a vassal of the Yuan from 1270 to 1356, 'a son-in-law kingdom'). 1260-1269: after the spring 1259 peace the shape is the 1227 one; Ssangseong, annexed by the Mongols in 1258, lies outside it.

New keyframe. The Mongols 'backed the rebellion of Goryeo officials in the northwest and created the Dongnyeong Prefecture' in the context of events around 1269-1270; 'Goryeo regained formal control of Dongnyeong in 1290'. The page names the north-west, not the prefecture's bounds: the whole Pyongan region is a reading (confidence 2).

correction.text: the 1227 shape plus North Pyongan, with the north-west back (Dongnyeong regained 1290); Ssangseong still Mongol

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: 'Goryeo regained formal control of Dongnyeong in 1290'. Ssangseong in the north-east stays with the Yuan until 1356 ('By 1356 Goryeo regained its lost northern territories'). Jeju is the Tamna dossier's island.

correction.text: the Cliopatria 1363 shape from 1356, without Jeju (Tamna)

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: the year the page gives for the recovery of the north under King Gongmin. Cliopatria's first post-Mongol shape starts in 1363 (207,189 km2) and is used for 1356-1362 with Jeju removed, because the Tamna dossier (jk-02-b) draws the island as Tamna until 1404. Confidence on the exact outline is low: the page names Ssangseong, not the Yalu bend. Fix round: the Gongmin of Goryeo page has only 'In 1356, the Goryeo army retook these provinces partly thanks to the defection of Yi Cha-ch'un' (the Ssangseong and Dongnyeong Prefectures the Mongols made) and an undated Liaoyang campaign; it names no Yalu, Chagang, Ryanggang or Hamgyong land, and the Ssangseong Prefecture page says only 'Ssangsŏng prefecture fell to Goryeo in 1356'. The 43,700 km2 this shape adds beyond goryeo_1290 plus Hamgyong-namdo (Chagang, Ryanggang, North Hamgyong, north South Pyongan) therefore remain Cliopatria's unverified reach (confidence 1).

207,189 km2. The infobox gives no area; the Korean peninsula is about 220,000 km2 and the shape reaches 41.5 N, so the size is plausible. Cliopatria folds Jeju into Goryeo here; the Tamna page keeps local autonomy to 1404 and the Tamna dossier keeps the island as Tamna's, so it is removed (a vassal tint in the ledger).

208,184 km2: same outline as 1363 plus about 1,000 km2. In 1370 'Goryeo had terminated its tributary relationship with the Yuan' and sent forces to the Ming border in Liaodong; no land was held there. Jeju removed as in 1363.

correction.text: the Cliopatria 1385 shape without Jeju; valid 1385-1392

keyframe_review.note: Cliopatria runs this shape to 1394 but the page ends Goryeo with the abdication of Gongyang on 12 July 1392 (infobox) and Joseon's establishment. Years change (to 1392) and Jeju is removed as in 1363.

ledger.note: 918: Wang Kon is crowned Taejo and restores the name Goryeo. Infobox 'Coronation of Taejo: 25 July 918'; 'Wang Kŏn was raised to the throne after Kung Ye was deposed' and 'moved the capital back to Kaesong' (the infobox lists Cheorwon 918-919 as the temporary seat). Taebong page: four generals overthrew Kung Ye in 918. Fix round: the region now includes Naju, as goryeo_918 does (Gyeon Hwon page: Wang Kon captured it in 910).
919: the court settles at Gaegyeong (Kaesong). Infobox: temporary capital Cheorwon (918-919).

region.text: the Silla capital and the Daegu area

ledger.note: 927: Later Baekje raids deep into Silla. 'Kyŏn Hwŏn sacked the Silla capital. Taejo suffered a defeat near Daegu.' Contest zone read as the Daegu area; the page gives no front line.

region.text: the Daegu and Andong area after Gochang

ledger.note: 930: Goryeo wins at Gochang. 'Victories over Later Baekje' in 930 and 934 (Goryeo page); Later Baekje page: the Battle of Gochang near Andong 'ended in a decisive Goryeo victory'. The year is the page's; 930 is read as the end of the contested phase in the north of Gyeongsang.

region.text: Silla's remaining 38,421 km2, the Gyeongsang region round Gyeongju

ledger.note: 935: Silla submits to Goryeo. 'the peaceful annexation of Later Silla in 935' (Goryeo page); Unified Silla infobox 'Handover to the Goryeo: 935'. Silla's rump (Gyeongsang) comes whole; the page gives no month.

region.text: Later Baekje: Jeolla and the south-west

ledger.note: 936: Goryeo conquers Later Baekje and ends the Later Three Kingdoms. 'Conquest of Later Baekje, 936' with an army of 87,500; Later Baekje page: 'finally fell in 936' (no month). Hubaekje's outline here includes Naju, which Goryeo already held since 918 (hubaekje drops it from 910); the overlap is about 2,500 km2 and mirrors hubaekje's dissolve region.

region.text: Jeju Island, the kingdom of Tamna

ledger.note: 938: Tamna becomes a Goryeo vassal. Tamna infobox 'Vassal state of Goryeo (938-1105)'; text 'subjugated by the Goryeo dynasty in 938, and officially annexed in 1105' but 'the kingdom maintained local autonomy until 1404'. Because the Tamna dossier keeps the island as Tamna's until 1404, the tint runs through the annexation of 1105 as 'local autonomous administration of Goryeo (1105-1275, 1301-1392)'.

region.text: the land between the Liao border and Goryeo up to the Yalu

ledger.note: 993: Goryeo takes the land up to the Yalu. 'Goryeo formally incorporated the land between the border of Liao and Goryeo up to the Yalu River, which was at the time occupied by Jurchen tribes' (Goryeo-Khitan War page, after negotiations led by Sŏ Hŭi). Goryeo page: 'Six Garrison Settlements East of the River' founded 994-996. Region read as North Pyongan. Fix round: the counterpart is now jurchens (was nobody) because the page says the land was 'occupied by Jurchen tribes'; Cliopatria's Liao shape also holds almost all of North Pyongan (about 18,000 of its 18,200 grid km2) for 993-1125 (and Great Jin 1130, Mongol Empire 1260), an overlap for ea-05 and ia-02 to remove; the page does not say Liao held it.

1014: Liao attacks across the Yalu. '1014-1017: Liao bridged the Yalu and attacked; Goryeo lost the Poju (Uiju) region.' The 993 and 1010 invasions did not hold ground (1010: the capital was 'sacked and burnt' and Hyeonjong fled to Naju), so the contest starts with the first campaign that kept land.

region.text: the Poju (Uiju) region at the mouth of the Yalu

ledger.note: 1014: the Poju (Uiju) region falls to Liao. 'Goryeo lost the Poju (Uiju) region' in the 1014-1017 attacks; Khitan War page: before 1018 Liao demanded 'surrender of the region of the Six Garrison Settlements'. Sinuiju stands for Uiju (the gazetteer lacks Uiju).

1022: peace with Liao. 'Goryeo adopted the Liao reign title in the fourth month' of 1022; the Khitans recognised the king and Goryeo acknowledged vassalage (the Liao suzerain event belongs to the Liao dossier). Bielenstein, quoted on the page, holds the two made peace as equals.

1031: Liao cedes the land round the Yalu. 'The Liao ceded territory around the Yalu to Goryeo' after Hyeonjong's death and his successor's investiture. Region read as the Poju area lost in 1014; Cheolli Jangseong (1033-1044) then ran 'from the mouth of the Yalu River to the east coast' (Goryeo page).

1104: the Jurchens beat Goryeo in the north-east. '1104: Im Kan's army defeated; Chongju taken by the Jurchens.' The Goryeo-Jurchen War is dated 1104-1109 in the infobox. Hamgyong-namdo stands for the Chongju region.

region.text: the Nine Fortresses, traditionally at Hamhung

ledger.note: 1107: Yun Gwan wins the north-east. 'in 1107, General Yun led the newly formed Goryeo army, a force of approximately 170 thousand men called Pyŏlmuban' and 'built nine fortresses to the northeast of the Goryeo-Jurchen borders'; Goryeo page: he set out in December. The page gives the traditional location as present-day Hamheung and adds that some sources put the fortresses in Manchuria.

1108: the Nine Fortresses go back to the Jurchens. 'In 1108, General Yun was given orders to withdraw his troops by Goryeo's new ruler, King Yejong' and the fortresses were 'returned to the Jurchens'; Goryeo page: returned to the Wanyan clan and 'exchanged for Poju' (the Poju side of this is unclear against the 1031 cession). Confidence 2 (reviewer jk-02-c): the Yun Gwan page names present-day Hamheung, not the province, and does not date the return itself; the 1108 year is the Goryeo page's ('handed back to the Jurchens').
1108: the Goryeo-Jurchen fighting ends with the withdrawal. The infobox runs the war 1104-1109.

region.text: North Pyongan, held by Mongol darughachis from 1232

ledger.note: 1231: the Mongols invade. 'On 26 August 1231, a Mongol force led by Saritai crossed the Yalu and surrounded Hamsin-chin (Uiju)'; by 1232 Mongol darughachis controlled 'almost all of modern North Pyongan Province'; Kaesong was surrounded in December 1231 and Goryeo submitted.
1232: the court flees to Ganghwa Island. 'The royal court moved to Ganghwado in the Bay of Gyeonggi in 1232' (Goryeo page; infobox 1232-1270). The Mongol darughachis were killed that summer.

1258: the Mongols create Ssangseong Prefecture in the north-east. After residents defected, 'They established Ssangsŏng Prefecture in their area' (Mongol invasions page); 'By 1356 Goryeo regained its lost northern territories such as the Ssangseong Prefecture' (Goryeo under Mongol rule). The page names the prefecture, not its extent; Hamgyong-namdo is a reading. Fix round: the Ssangseong Prefecture page puts it 'in modern-day Kumya County, South Hamgyong Province' and names no extent, and Goryeo's keyframes stop at 39.45 N, so this loss removes only 1 grid cell (250 km2) and the annexation is nearly invisible on the map; a Hwaju strip south of the Cheolli wall is not added because no page opened gives its bounds (the page does name 'Cheollyeong Pass', north of which the land went to the Yuan).

1259: peace with the Mongols. 'In the spring of 1259, a peace agreement was concluded'; the crown prince (later Wonjong) went to the Mongol court. Goryeo became a vassal of the Mongols/Yuan ('for approximately 80 years', ending 1356), recorded by the suzerain.
1270: the court returns from Ganghwa to Gaegyeong (infobox 'Ganghwa (1232-1270)'; Wonjong's reign).

region.text: the north-west, Dongnyeong Prefecture: the Pyongan region within the land Goryeo's keyframes hold (Cliopatria 1227 plus North Pyongan)

ledger.note: 1270: the Mongols create Dongnyeong Prefecture in the north-west. They 'backed the rebellion' of Goryeo officials in the north-west and 'created the Dongnyeong Prefecture' (events of c.1269-1270). The page does not give its bounds; the Pyongan region is a reading. Fix round: the region is cut to the land goryeo_1227 holds; {region Pyongan} alone is 64,000 km2 (Chagang and South Pyongan included) against 29,800 km2 drawn.

1275: the Yuan take Jeju. Tamna infobox 'Local autonomous administration of Yuan dynasty as Tamna Prefecture (1275-1301)'. Goryeo forces had defeated the Jeju rebels of the Sambyeolcho in 1273 (Goryeo under Mongol rule).

region.text: the north-west, Dongnyeong Prefecture: the Pyongan region within the land Goryeo's keyframes hold (Cliopatria 1227 plus North Pyongan)

ledger.note: 1290: Dongnyeong returns to Goryeo. 'Goryeo regained formal control of Dongnyeong in 1290'. Fix round: region cut as in the 1270 loss, so the gain matches goryeo_1290. The Gongmin of Goryeo page puts 'these provinces' (Ssangseong and Dongnyeong) in 1356 ('In 1356, the Goryeo army retook these provinces partly thanks to the defection of Yi Cha-ch'un'); the Goryeo under Mongol rule page's 1290 is kept.

1294: Jeju is Goryeo's again. 'Goryeo regained formal control of ... Jeju in 1294' but 'the Jeju military command remained outside of their jurisdiction'. The Tamna infobox gives 1301 for the end of the Yuan Tamna Prefecture ('1301-1392' local autonomous administration of Goryeo): a disagreement of seven years between the two pages.

1356: King Gongmin regains the north. 'By 1356 Goryeo under King Gongmin regained its lost northern territories such as the Ssangseong Prefecture' (Goryeo page: 'Conquest of Liaoyang' in 1356 and Red Turban invasions repulsed in 1359 and 1360). Fix round: Gongmin of Goryeo page: 'In 1356, the Goryeo army retook these provinces partly thanks to the defection of Yi Cha-ch'un' (the Ssangseong and Dongnyeong Prefectures); Ssangseong Prefecture page: 'Ssangsŏng prefecture fell to Goryeo in 1356'.
1382: the court moves to Hanyang (infobox 'Hanyang (1382-1383, 1390-1391)').
1383: back to Gaegyeong, read from the infobox span 1382-1383.
1390: the court moves to Hanyang again (infobox 1390-1391).
1391: back to Gaegyeong, read from the infobox span 1390-1391.
1392: Goryeo's lordship over Tamna ends with Goryeo; Joseon places the island under 'firm central control' in 1404 (Tamna page).

region.text: all of Goryeo, taken over whole by Joseon

ledger.note: 1392: Yi Sŏnggye ends Goryeo. 'Abdication of Gongyang: 12 July 1392'; in 1388 Yi 'stopped at the border and rebelled' instead of invading Liaodong (Wihwado Retreat), and in 1392 he 'put to death the last three Goryeo kings' and established Joseon.

wars.name: Later Three Kingdoms (Goryeo phase)

zones.text: the Daegu area, where Taejo was beaten in 927, and Gochang near Andong in 930

wars.outcome: Goryeo won: Silla submitted in 935 and Later Baekje fell in 936.
wars.note: Goryeo page: 927 Gyeongju sacked and Taejo beaten near Daegu; victories in 930 and 934; 935 annexation of Silla; 936 conquest of Later Baekje with 87,500 men.

wars.name: Khitan invasions of Goryeo
wars.outcome: The Khitan invaders were finished off by allied Mongol-Goryeo forces in 1219.

wars.name: Goryeo-Khitan War

zones.text: the north-west frontier between the Yalu and the Chongchon

wars.outcome: Liao won the first two invasions (993, 1010; the capital was burnt in 1010) and lost the third (1018-1019, Gwiju). Peace and Goryeo's vassalage in 1022; Goryeo took the land to the Yalu in 993 and the Yalu area was ceded in 1031.
wars.note: Infobox: Date '993, 1010, 1018-1019'. The page places the Battle of Gwiju in 1018 (infobox third invasion 1018-1019).

wars.name: Goryeo-Jurchen War

zones.text: Chongju and the Hamhung plain, the Nine Fortresses

wars.outcome: The Jurchens won in 1104; Yun Gwan built nine fortresses in 1107; they were returned in 1108.
wars.note: The Wikipedia article 'Goryeo-Jurchen War' would not load (two URL forms); the dates are from the Goryeo infobox label 1104-1109 and the Yun Gwan page.

wars.name: Mongol invasions of Korea

zones.text: North Pyongan under Mongol darughachis from 1232

wars.outcome: Mongol victory: six major campaigns (1231, 1232, 1235, 1238, 1247, 1253) and the 1258 Ssangseong Prefecture; Goryeo sued for peace in the spring of 1259 and became a Mongol vassal.
wars.note: Campaigns reached Chungju (1253) and the Southern Capital (1236); the contested zone is only the land the Mongols held.

wars.name: Sambyeolcho Rebellion

zones.text: Jeju, where Goryeo forces defeated the rebels in 1273

wars.outcome: The rebels, officials who resisted in the islands off the southern shore, were beaten on Jeju in 1273 (the Tamna page dates the rebellion to 1274).
wars.note: Needs its own dossier if it held land for a year or more.

wars.name: Red Turban invasions of Goryeo
wars.outcome: Goryeo repulsed the Red Turban invasions of 1359 and 1360.

wars.name: Wihwado Retreat
wars.outcome: Yi Sŏnggye stopped the planned invasion of Liaoning at Wihwado and turned on the court; Joseon followed in 1392.

certainty.note: Frontiers with Later Baekje, Silla, the Jurchens and the Khitans are approximate; the Yalu line of 993 is a stated limit but the page gives no survey.
The northern frontier is the Cheolli Jangseong wall 'from the mouth of the Yalu River to the east coast' (1033-1044); the north-east beyond it and the 1104-1108 Jurchen swing are soft.
Mongol-held and contested land (North Pyongan 1231-1259, Ssangseong 1258-1356, Dongnyeong 1270-1290) has no stated boundary; Jeju is a separate state under a vassal tint.

notes:
Seven keyframes are new or re-dated. Cliopatria's Goryeo row has no shape for 1260-1362 (the Mongol overlordship), starts in 922 although the page dates the founding to 918, ends in 1394 although Goryeo ended on 12 July 1392, and never reaches the Yalu. Fixes: goryeo_918, goryeo_993 (+North Pyongan), goryeo_1260, 1270, 1290, 1356. Jeju is removed from the 1363-1385 shapes because the Tamna dossier keeps the island as Tamna's (vassal tint) to 1404; the Goryeo page says it was 'incorporated into Goryeo in 1105' but the Tamna page says local autonomy continued.
Not recorded here because the suzerain owns the event (a vassal_start with counterpart goryeo in the suzerain's dossier): Goryeo as a Liao vassal from 1022 (Khitan War page: 'declaration of vassalage', Liao reign title adopted in the fourth month of 1022; Bielenstein: peace as equals), as a Jin vassal from 1126 (Goryeo page: 'Goryeo's king declared himself a Jin vassal (tributary)'; Cliopatria relation 1126-1235; the end year is not on the pages opened), as a Mongol/Yuan vassal from 1259 (peace, crown prince to the court) or 1270 (infobox 'vassal of the Yuan 1270-1356', 'son-in-law kingdom') to 1356; the 1370 end of the tributary relationship with the Yuan is on the Goryeo under Mongol rule page. The Ming relation 1368-1392 is not described on the pages opened. Counterpart slugs for the suzerain files: liao-dynasty (ea-05), great-jin (ea-05), mongol-empire (ia-02), yuan-dynasty (ea-06), ming-dynasty (ea-07).
Pages: 6 opened against a budget of 5 (the Tamna page was added for the 938/1105/1275/1294 relation). 'Goryeo-Jurchen War' would not load at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goryeo%E2%80%93Jurchen_War or https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goryeo-Jurchen_War; the Yun Gwan page and the Goryeo infobox stand in. The Goryeo and Taebong pages carry no area, so no infobox/Cliopatria area comparison was possible. Disagreements: Jeju regained 1294 (Goryeo under Mongol rule) vs 1301 (Tamna infobox); Kaesong sacked 1010 (Goryeo and Khitan War pages); the Goryeo page's 1108 'exchanged for Poju' against the 1031 cession.
Not on any page opened and therefore not recorded: the 1135 Myoch'ŏng rebellion's land (a possible rebel state 'Daewi'), the Jurchen Nine Fortresses' exact bounds, the Ming-Goryeo Tieling dispute of 1387-1388, Dongnyeong's real extent. Gazetteer: Cheorwon is missing as a place (coordinates used). Fix round (2026-10-19): (1) Naju added to goryeo_918 and the found event, goryeo_922 now adjust (Naju was nobody's 918-935 otherwise; Gyeon Hwon page). (2) The 1270 loss and 1290 gain of Dongnyeong are cut to the Pyongan land the keyframes hold (about 29,800 km2, not 64,000). (3) The 993 gain's counterpart is jurchens (Goryeo-Khitan War page: land 'occupied by Jurchen tribes'); the Liao overlap of North Pyongan 993-1125 is for ea-05. (4) Predecessors now list unified-silla and hubaekje. (5) 1258: the annexation of Ssangseong is nearly invisible because the keyframes stop at 39.45 N; the Ssangseong Prefecture page gives only Kumya County and no extent, so nothing was added. (6) Disagreement left open: the Gongmin of Goryeo page has the Ssangseong and Dongnyeong provinces retaken in 1356, the Goryeo under Mongol rule page has Dongnyeong back in 1290 (kept). goryeo_1356 remains a low-confidence Cliopatria reach (Gongmin page names no Yalu, Chagang or Ryanggang land). The Nine Fortresses' extent is still on no page (the Ssangseong Prefecture page is silent).
